week_headline: Brain health takes centre stage as new research suggests lifestyle habits may buffer early Alzheimer's damage more than previously thought

claims.verdict: There's genuinely solid evidence here — the concept of 'cognitive reserve' is well established, meaning that keeping your brain active and healthy throughout life can delay when Alzheimer's symptoms become noticeable, even as the underlying disease progresses. Importantly though, this is not a cure or a prevention of the disease itself — it's more like having a larger buffer before the effects show up in daily life. Diet, exercise, sleep, social engagement, and mental stimulation all contribute, but no single habit is a silver bullet.
claims.verdict_highlight: Cognitive reserve buys time, not a cure
sources: NIH National Institute on Aging — Cognitive Reserve and Alzheimer's Disease
Lancet Commission on Dementia Prevention, Intervention and Care (2020)
NEJM — Lifestyle Factors and Risk of Alzheimer's Disease
Harvard Health Publishing — Building a Resilient Brain
JAMA Neurology — Brain Maintenance and Cognitive Aging
claims.global_opinion: In the US, the NIH actively funds cognitive reserve research and public health campaigns promote brain-healthy lifestyles as part of dementia strategy. In the UK, the NHS and Alzheimer's Society both endorse lifestyle interventions but are careful to frame them as risk-reduction rather than prevention, to avoid false hope. In Japan, where dementia rates are closely monitored given the ageing population, community-based programmes combining physical activity and social engagement are widely promoted as standard public health policy.
claims.brit_take: Essentially, keeping your brain busy with crosswords, walks, and a decent chat over tea won't stop Alzheimer's — but it does seem to give your brain a bit more runway before things get tricky.
claims.claim: Healthy brain maintenance protects cognitive skills from early Alzheimer effects
